title: Eater World's Fare Brought 20 Nations of Food to NYC During World Cup Weekend
excerpt: Eater's largest festival transformed Pier 36 into a global culinary destination with pop-ups from Dominique Ansel, Sushi Noz, and dozens more during the FIFA World Cup.
body:
• Eater World's Fare, Eater's largest festival ever, drew more than 6,000 guests to Pier 36 in New York City on July 18 during the FIFA World Cup.
  • The event featured restaurant pop-ups representing over 20 nations, with appearances from chefs Shota Nakajima and Calvin Eng alongside restaurants including Dominique Ansel, Sushi Noz, and José Andrés Group's Mercado Little Spain.
  • General admission tickets started at $30, with VIP packages presented by Cathay Pacific offering exclusive chef-crafted dishes and an open bar.
  • Produced by Medium Rare, the festival drew inspiration from historic world's fairs to celebrate global food culture alongside the world's biggest sporting event.

A World's Fair for the Food Generation

Eater World's Fare landed at Pier 36 on Manhattan's Lower East Side on Saturday, July 18, timed to coincide with the FIFA World Cup weekend in New York City. The festival, billed as Eater's largest event to date, brought together dozens of restaurant pop-ups and culinary experiences representing more than 20 countries under one roof.

The concept drew from the spirit of historic world's fairs — events that once united nations through culture and innovation — and repackaged it for a food-obsessed generation. More than 6,000 guests were expected to pass through the venue, sampling bites from some of New York's most celebrated restaurants alongside international flavors curated by Eater's editorial team.

"New York is arguably the most global city in the world, particularly when it comes to the diversity of its communities and cuisines. We wanted to create an experience that brings together the very best of food and sports."

— Stephanie Wu, Eater Editor-in-Chief

The Lineup: From Sushi Noz to South Philly Barbacoa

The culinary programming read like a greatest-hits list of New York dining. Chefs Shota Nakajima and Calvin Eng headlined the event, with Eng creating Hong Kong-inspired dishes in collaboration with Cathay Pacific. The restaurant roster included Mokbar, Golden HOF, Caffe Panna, Dominique Ansel, Charles Pan Fried Chicken, Banh Anh Em, South Philly Barbacoa, Zaab Zaab, Court Street Grocers, Frank Pepe Pizzeria Napoletana, José Andrés Group's Mercado Little Spain, Sushi Noz, Gourmega, Parm, Mimi Cheng's, Sally's Apizza, Pecking House, Gotham Burger Social Club, and Fan Fan Doughnuts.

Gourmega, from the minds behind the acclaimed Ghetto Gastro collective, operated a dedicated pop-up powered by Square, offering free bites to festival-goers. Maruchan presented an exclusive ramen experience with Nakajima, showcasing global noodle traditions through a series of unique ramen samples inspired by different countries.

Beyond the Food: Brands and Experiences

The festival extended well beyond restaurant stalls. Cathay Pacific, the Hong Kong-based airline, anchored the "Gateway to Asia" experience, transporting guests across the continent through curated tastings inspired by destinations including Thailand and the Philippines. Attending guests who signed up as Cathay members had a chance to win two Business class tickets to Hong Kong.

Dole created a tropical sampling station, S.Pellegrino hosted water-and-food harmonization tastings for VIP guests, and Lifeway Foods set up an oversized inflatable kefir bottle where guests could kick soccer balls through the display. Milagro Tequila operated branded bars throughout the venue mixing cocktails from its 100% blue agave lineup.

General admission tickets started at $30 and included access to all festival programming, live demonstrations, and complimentary bites from sponsor partners. VIP packages, presented by Cathay Pacific, added early access, a private lounge modeled on the airline's First and Business class lounges, an open bar, and exclusive dishes from top chefs.

Where Food Meets the Beautiful Game

The timing was no accident. With the FIFA World Cup underway in the United States, New York was flooded with international visitors and soccer fans — exactly the audience for a festival celebrating global cuisine. Medium Rare, the experiential entertainment company behind events like John Summit's Experts Only Festival, Kelce Jam, and Guy Fieri's Flavortown Tailgate, produced the event.

"What unites the world more than sports? Food. We've spent years building experiences around moments that feel genuinely unrepeatable, and bringing together the flavors of the world during one of the biggest global sporting weekends in the most restaurant-obsessed city in America felt like the perfect opportunity."

— Adam Richman, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Medium Rare

A Template for the Diaspora Food Scene

For the Indian diaspora in the tri-state area and beyond, the festival's global scope — spanning flavors from Southeast Asia to Latin America to the Middle East — reflects a broader trend of food events that celebrate immigrant culinary traditions alongside established restaurant culture. With South Asian flavors increasingly prominent in New York's dining landscape, events like Eater World's Fare signal how mainstream food culture is catching up to the diversity that immigrant communities have long brought to American cities.
nri_angle: The festival's celebration of immigrant culinary traditions across 20+ nations mirrors the food diversity that South Asian and other diaspora communities bring to American cities.
